description: Cortés's rivalry with Velázquez, his Mexican expedition and the massacres that opened Tenochtitlán.
content_html:
Hernán Cortés: The Man and His Mission

Hernán Cortés was born in Medellin, Extremadura, Spain, in 1485. He arrived in Hispaniola in 1504 and Cuba in 1511, where he served as a secretary to Governor Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar. By 1518 he had been authorised to lead an expedition to the Mexican mainland, following reports of a rich civilisation from earlier Spanish forays. Then, at the last moment, Diego Velázquez withdrew the authorisation, suspecting Cortés was too ambitious and would not remain under his control.

Cortés defied the order. In February 1519 he set out from Cuba with approximately eleven ships, around 500–600 soldiers, sixteen horses and a handful of artillery pieces. It was an act of insubordination that put him in legal jeopardy — he was operating without royal authority and could be arrested. His strategy was to succeed so spectacularly that the Spanish crown would confirm his authority retroactively. He wrote long, self-justifying letters (the Cartas de Relación) directly to King Charles I, bypassing Velázquez entirely.

Key Fact

Cortés defied Governor Velázquez’s last-minute withdrawal of authorisation and sailed from Cuba in February 1519. He wrote directly to King Charles I to justify himself, hoping military success would secure royal backing.

Landing on the Mexican Coast

Cortés landed on the Mexican coast at the site of modern Veracruz in April 1519. Here he made one of his most consequential decisions: he scuttled (or according to some accounts, beached and dismantled) his own ships to prevent his men from retreating to Cuba. With no way back, his force was committed. He also received a crucial gift at this point: a woman named La Malinche (also known as Malintzin or Doña Marina), who had been presented to him as part of a gift of enslaved women. She spoke both Nahuatl (the Aztec language) and Maya, and could communicate via a chain of interpretation that allowed Cortés to negotiate with indigenous peoples. Without her, the conquest would have been far more difficult.

La Malinche’s role has been interpreted very differently by later historians. Spanish chroniclers praised her as essential to Cortés’s success. Some later Mexican nationalists condemned her as a traitor who helped destroy Aztec civilisation. Modern historians tend to see her as a woman who had been enslaved and sold by her own people, who made strategic choices to survive. She bore Cortés a son, Martín Cortés, often described as one of the first mestizo (mixed European-indigenous) people recorded in colonial records. She is a powerful example of the contested nature of historical memory around the conquest.

Alliances with Indigenous Peoples

Cortés’s most important strategic achievement was forging alliances with peoples who resented Aztec rule. The Tlaxcalans were one of the few peoples who had successfully resisted Aztec conquest — they had been deliberately left unconquered to supply sacrificial captives through the Flower Wars. When Cortés arrived, they initially fought him in a series of fierce battles but, having tested his military strength and found it formidable, negotiated an alliance. The Tlaxcalans would supply the vast majority of the soldiers in the eventual siege of Tenochtitlán — some estimates put their contribution at tens of thousands of warriors compared to a few hundred Spaniards.

The Totonacs of the Gulf Coast also allied with Cortés, eager to escape Aztec tribute obligations. Cortés encouraged subject peoples to withhold tribute from the Aztecs, positioning himself as a liberator rather than a conqueror. This framing was partly genuine and partly cynical; the peoples who allied with him would soon find themselves under a different form of domination.

Key Fact

The Tlaxcalans were traditional enemies of the Aztecs who had resisted incorporation into the empire. Their alliance with Cortés provided the bulk of the military force used against Tenochtitlán; without Tlaxcalan warriors, the Spanish could not have conquered the Aztec Empire.

The Massacre at Cholula, 1519

On the march to Tenochtitlán, Cortés reached Cholula — a major religious city and one of the most sacred sites in Mexico. What happened there in October 1519 is one of the most debated events of the conquest. The Spanish and their Tlaxcalan allies carried out a large-scale massacre of Cholulan nobles and warriors gathered in the main courtyard. The death toll reported in Spanish accounts (including Cortés’s own letter) ranged from around 3,000 to 6,000; some scholars suggest the figures were exaggerated.

Cortés justified the massacre by claiming he had discovered an Aztec-backed plot to ambush his force. Indigenous accounts of the events differ significantly — some suggest the Tlaxcalans encouraged the violence to settle old scores with Cholula. Whatever the truth, the Cholula massacre sent a clear message to other cities on the road to Tenochtitlán: resistance would be met with overwhelming violence. It also revealed Cortés’s willingness to use terror as a political tool.

Moctezuma II (also spelled Montezuma) received Cortés peacefully at the entrance to Tenochtitlán on 8 November 1519. The reasons for this reception are debated. Early colonial-era sources suggest Moctezuma believed Cortés was the returning god Quetzalcoatl; most modern historians argue this account was shaped by post-conquest indigenous politics and may not reflect what Moctezuma actually thought. More likely, he was applying a diplomatic strategy — welcoming a potentially powerful ally while assessing the threat. Whatever his reasoning, the decision to allow the Spanish into the capital proved fatal to the empire.
exam_tip_html: For 5-mark source utility questions about the conquest, remember to address content, provenance and contextual knowledge. Cortés’s own letters (Cartas de Relación) are a key source — useful for showing Spanish perspectives and justifications, but written to impress King Charles I and secure royal backing, so they exaggerate successes and downplay brutality. For 6-mark cause/consequence questions, avoid just describing what happened: explain the causal mechanism explicitly (“This caused X because…”).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cortés defied Governor Velázquez’s last-minute withdrawal of authorisation and sailed for Mexico in February 1519 with about 500–600 soldiers; he scuttled his ships on arrival to prevent retreat and wrote directly to King Charles I to justify himself.
  • His most important asset was La Malinche, his Nahuatl-Maya interpreter, and his alliances with anti-Aztec peoples: the Tlaxcalans and Totonacs provided the bulk of his military force and made the eventual conquest possible.
  • The Cholula massacre (October 1519) demonstrated Cortés’s use of terror as a political tool; Moctezuma II then received him peacefully into Tenochtitlán in November 1519, a decision that led directly to the fall of the empire.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Cortés’s relationship with Governor Velázquez before the 1519 expedition.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. Velázquez originally authorised then withdrew permission for the expedition / Cortés defied Velázquez and sailed anyway / Velázquez feared Cortés would act independently). Two marks for a developed explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of La Malinche’s role in the conquest of Mexico.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• She served as Cortés’s interpreter, speaking both Nahuatl and Maya, enabling him to negotiate with indigenous peoples.
• She acted as a diplomatic adviser, helping Cortés understand Aztec politics and customs.
• She bore Cortés a son, Martín Cortés, one of the first recorded mestizo children.
• Without her linguistic skills, Cortés could not have forged the alliances that made the conquest possible.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Tlaxcalan alliance with Cortés in 1519.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that the Tlaxcalans were traditional enemies of the Aztecs who had resisted incorporation into the empire and were deliberately kept unconquered to supply sacrificial captives through the Flower Wars; their resentment of Aztec domination made them willing to ally with Cortés once he demonstrated military power; develops with specific evidence.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Cholula massacre (1519) for the Spanish campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the massacre sent a message of overwhelming force to other cities on the road to Tenochtitlán, reducing resistance; or that it revealed Cortés’s use of terror as a political tool and shaped how the conquest proceeded; links specifically to the subsequent peaceful reception at Tenochtitlán.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Cortés’s alliances with indigenous peoples for the conquest of the Aztec Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (Tlaxcalans and Totonacs provided the bulk of the military force; without them, a force of ~500 Spaniards could not have defeated an empire of millions; alliances exploited genuine anti-Aztec resentment) AND over time (the conquest model of exploiting internal divisions was repeated across the Americas; indigenous allies suffered under Spanish rule despite helping to bring it about). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may lack full over-time analysis.
Developing: Describes alliances without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Cortés’s personal qualities were more important than his alliances in making the conquest of Mexico possible.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Cortés showed exceptional decisiveness (defying Velázquez, scuttling ships, writing to the king directly).
• His use of La Malinche as interpreter and diplomat shows his skill at exploiting available resources.
• His strategic use of terror (Cholula) and diplomacy in alternation controlled the campaign.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Without Tlaxcalan and Totonac allies providing tens of thousands of warriors, the conquest would have been impossible for ~500 Spaniards.
• Aztec vulnerabilities — tribute resentment, internal divisions — were structural advantages Cortés exploited but did not create.
• Disease (smallpox) would prove the decisive factor in the siege, beyond any individual’s control.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Why did Cortés defy Governor Velázquez's orders in February 1519?
options: Because the king of Spain ordered him to sail immediately
Because Velázquez withdrew authorisation for the expedition at the last minute, fearing Cortés would act independently
Because Velázquez was arrested by Spanish authorities
Because Cortés had already bought his ships and could not return them

knowledge_checks.q: What was La Malinche's key role in Cortés's expedition?
options: She commanded Tlaxcalan warriors in battle
She negotiated the Treaty of Tordesillas
She wrote the Cartas de Relación for Cortés
She served as interpreter, speaking both Nahuatl and Maya

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ were traditional enemies of the Aztecs who provided Cortés with his most important indigenous military alliance.
Cortés scuttled his own ships on the Mexican coast in 1519 in order to _____.
options: prevent his men from retreating to Cuba
prevent the Aztecs from stealing them
obey Velázquez's orders to return to Cuba
create timber for fortifications at Veracruz

knowledge_checks.q: Match each person to their role in the conquest of Mexico:
right: Governor of Cuba who originally authorised then withdrew Cortés's expedition
Nahuatl-Maya interpreter and diplomatic adviser to Cortés
Aztec emperor who received Cortés peacefully into Tenochtitlán in 1519

glossary_terms.definition: Spanish conquistador (1485–1547) who led the expedition that conquered the Aztec Empire between 1519 and 1521.
Spanish governor of Cuba (1465–1524) who originally authorised but then attempted to cancel Cortés's expedition, fearing he would act independently.
Indigenous woman (also known as Malintzin or Doña Marina) who served as Cortés's interpreter and diplomatic adviser, speaking both Nahuatl and Maya.
A powerful indigenous people of central Mexico, enemies of the Aztecs, who allied with Cortés in 1519 and provided the bulk of the military force against Tenochtitlán.
An indigenous people of the Gulf Coast of Mexico who were subject to Aztec tribute demands and allied with Cortés in 1519.
The ninth Aztec emperor (ruled c.1502–1520) who received Cortés into Tenochtitlán in November 1519 and was later taken hostage by the Spanish.
